notes.location: Article introduction and Kvant-1 incident account
notes.summary: On 24 February 1997, a solid-fuel oxygen-generator canister ignited in Mir's Kvant-1 module. The fire produced dense smoke and blocked access to one Soyuz escape craft while six crew members were aboard.

Mir crew members used oxygen masks and foam extinguishers during the 1997 fire. The flame ultimately went out, and the station's life-support system cleared the smoke over the following hours. This was an incident, not a controlled experiment.
On 27 January 1967, an AS-204 preflight test ended in a command-module fire that killed astronauts Grissom, White and Chaffee. The cabin was pressurized with pure oxygen during the test.
The Apollo 1 review did not identify one definite ignition source. NASA later changed the command-module hatch and restricted combustible cabin materials.
An oxygen-tank explosion damaged Apollo 13's oxygen and fuel-cell systems during flight and ended the planned lunar landing. This was a spacecraft-system accident, not a controlled flame experiment.

notes.location: Archived Combustion Experiments and Combustion Integrated Rack
notes.summary: NASA's combustion programme page lists FLEX, BASS, Saffire, SAME and SPICE among archived investigations. It describes the Combustion Integrated Rack as an International Space Station facility dedicated to combustion research.
NASA's combustion research guide explains that reduced gravity suppresses buoyancy, simplifying some flame analyses. It identifies spacecraft fire safety as a concern for exploration missions.

A NASA Spinoff entry describes an incipient fire detector used in space shuttle orbiters that sampled airborne combustion particles and distinguished them from dust. This is a technology-transfer account, not an experiment result.
A NASA Spinoff entry describes a Johnson Space Center collaboration on lighter firefighter air tanks. This is a technology-transfer account, not a spacecraft fire experiment.
A NASA Spinoff entry describes Project FIRES, a NASA and FEMA effort applying Apollo-era materials and design ideas to firefighter protective gear. This is a technology-transfer account.
